extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate discrete mathematics instructors and students (classroom project/worksheet users)
extracted.subtask_description: Worksheet and instructor notes for classroom-tested discrete math projects: constructing affine planes from MOLS, playing/analyzing tic-tac-toe on finite affine planes, and exploring the Josephus problem to teach recursion, induction, binary and modular ideas. Material is aimed at single-class activities and follow-up course connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms of an affine plane
rubrics_metrics.description: An affine plane is a nonempty set of points, P, and a nonempty collection of subsets of points (called lines) which satisfy the following three axioms: (1) through any two distinct points there exists a unique line; (2) if p is a point, ` is a line, and p is not on line `, then there exists a unique line, m, that passes through p and is parallel to `; (3) there are at least two points on each line, and there are at least two lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three axioms are the verification criteria for any candidate finite plane. Exercises ask students to verify these axioms for constructed examples (e.g., the affine planes of orders 3 and 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing an affine plane from MOLS
rubrics_metrics.description: In each Latin square, the points corresponding to identical symbols form a line. Use vertical and horizontal lines plus one line per Latin square (symbols matched across squares) to produce the full set of lines of the affine plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure given in exercises 1.8–1.10: place n^2 points in an n×n array, draw vertical and horizontal lines, then for each Latin square connect the points that carry the same symbol (use different colors for visibility). This method constructs the representative diagram of the affine plane of order n from a set of MOLS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin square property
rubrics_metrics.description: A Latin square is an n×n array in which each symbol appears exactly once in each row and exactly once in each column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.11 instructs students to 'show that L_k is a Latin square, that is, show that each element appears once in each row and column.' The Orthogonal Construction must produce Latin squares to be valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonality of Latin squares (MOLS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two Latin squares L_k and L_j are orthogonal if, when superimposed, each ordered pair of symbols (from L_k,L_j) appears exactly once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.11 asks to 'prove that if p is a prime then L_k and L_j are orthogonal by showing that each ordered pair is represented exactly once.' Orthogonality is required to extract the additional (non-horizontal/vertical) lines of the affine plane from MOLS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonal Construction correctness condition (prime criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Orthogonal Construction technique produces p−1 MOLS of order p if and only if p is a prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch provided: show L_k are Latin squares and pairwise orthogonal when p is prime (using modular arithmetic uniqueness); show construction fails (does not always produce Latin squares) when p is not prime. Exercises ask students to prove both directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural/counting properties of a finite affine plane of order n
rubrics_metrics.description: In an affine plane of order n: there are n^2 points; there are n^2 + n lines; each line contains n points; through any point there are n + 1 lines; any two non-parallel lines meet in exactly one point; the number of lines parallel to any given line is n (note: every line is parallel to itself); there are n + 1 parallel classes (each class consisting of n parallel lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are guided to fill a table for orders 2,3,4,5,7 and generalize to order n. These counts are used to relate the plane to an n×n grid and to reason about game outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual/representative construction guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When drawing representative diagrams of finite affine planes, connected points are used to represent lines (connected segments need not be geometrically straight), and intersections in the drawing do not necessarily indicate common points of the underlying plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: use colors for different lines, label points for reference; ensure you interpret intersections carefully (some crossing lines in the picture may not share a point in the combinatorial plane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise-based construction checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete tasks for students: Exercise 1.8 (construct affine plane of order 4 from 3 MOLS of order 4), Exercise 1.9 (order 5), Exercise 1.10 (use Orthogonal Construction to produce 6 MOLS of order 7 and draw corresponding plane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each exercise explicitly instructs placement of points, drawing of vertical/horizontal lines, and connecting points sharing symbols in the MOLS; use different colors for visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and rules for playing tic-tac-toe on an affine plane
rubrics_metrics.description: Tic-tac-toe is played on the affine plane of order n: players alternately mark points; a player wins by marking all points on any line of the plane. X always moves first and subscripts denote move order (X2 is the second X move).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On (ℤ_3) affine plane there are 12 winning lines; in general each line of the plane is a winning line. Students are instructed to play multiple games and to analyze outcomes on planes of different orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-move symmetry property
rubrics_metrics.description: On any affine plane every point lies on the same number of lines, so there is no geometric advantage to any particular first-point choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with standard 3×3 tic-tac-toe (center/corner asymmetry). The worksheet uses this to reason about strategy simplifications: X1 and O1 may be assumed arbitrary when analyzing outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known game-theoretic outcomes by plane order
rubrics_metrics.description: Determined outcomes: order 2 — X has a winning strategy (X wins on second move); order 3 — X has a winning strategy (explicit move sequence reasoning provided); order 4 — X has a winning strategy but the explicit human-playable algorithm is complex (computer search was used to show X can force a win); orders ≥5 (including 5 and 7 constructed earlier) — player O can force a draw (second player can force draw for all orders greater than 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet supplies reasoning for small orders (constructive proofs) and mentions that weight-function techniques prove draws for orders >4; order 10 MOLS nonexistence is cited as an example of combinatorial difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for demonstrating a winning strategy (affine plane of order 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show X has a winning strategy on (ℤ_3) plane: assume X1 and O1 arbitrary, choose X2 not on line containing X1 and O1, force O2 onto line X1X2; X3 blocks O1O2, O must block one of two threat-lines, then X4 completes the unblocked line and wins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet gives this explicit line-of-play reasoning as an example of proving X can always win by prescribing a move-selection method (strategy proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Known existence results and combinatorial difficulty for complete sets of MOLS
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete set of MOLS exists for all orders p^k where p is prime and k a positive integer; it is unknown whether complete sets exist for any other orders. It is known there is no complete set for order 10 (proof required heavy computation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contextualizes why constructing complete sets is hard and motivates exploration of Orthogonal Construction for prime orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design considerations for Josephus classroom activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities intended to be completed by students in a single class period early in the semester; can be done with pencil-and-paper or via role play; useful as an opening student-centered problem and as source material for later course topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor notes recommend role-playing to surface issues like 'who starts' and to act as an icebreaker; pencil-and-paper is acceptable if time is limited. Follow-up links to CS exercises (circular linked lists) and binary/modular arithmetic are suggested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and reduction ('using-what-came-before') recursion strategy for Josephus
rubrics_metrics.description: Define J(n,k) as the position of the last person left with n players eliminating every k-th person. The reduction technique: after the first removal, the remainder is an instance with fewer players and an adjusted starting position; use known J-values for smaller n to obtain J(n,k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet illustrates with examples: deducing J(12,3) from J(11,3) by tracking who becomes new starting player after the first elimination; students are asked to fill tables and observe patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary cyclic-left-shift method for skip=2 Josephus games
rubrics_metrics.description: For the Josephus problem with skip number 2, representing numbers in binary and performing a cyclic left shift of the leading 1 gives the position of the survivor: the cyclic left shift of the binary representation of 2^n + k is the binary representation of 2k+1, which yields the last person left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet frames this as an application connecting binary numeral properties to the survivor position and suggests using it to motivate binary number study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connections to mathematical topics (learning goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Josephus activities are intended to illustrate and provide exercises in recursion, mathematical induction, binary representations, and modular arithmetic; also suitable as programming exercises and for demonstrating circular linked lists in computer science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific suggested problems: (a) prove by induction survival pattern for skip=2 with 2n players; (b) generalize for 2n with k removed; (c) show the cyclic-left-shift relation; (d) make modular-arithmetic analogies. Bibliography and web resources are provided.
